etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English trouthe, truthe, trewthe, treowthe, from Old English trēowþ, trīewþ (“truth, veracity, faith, fidelity, loyalty, honour, pledge, covenant”), from Proto-Germanic *triwwiþō (“promise, covenant, contract”), from Proto-Indo-European *drū- (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *deru- (“firm, solid”), equivalent to true +‎ -th. Cognate with Norwegian trygd (“trustworthiness, security, insurance”), Icelandic tryggð (“loyalty, fidelity”).

definitions.definition: True facts, genuine depiction or statements of reality.

quote.citation: 1831 December 27, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, “Beauty—Genius”, in H[enry] N[elson] C[oleridge], editor, Specimens of the Table Talk of the Late Samuel Taylor Coleridge. […], volume II, London: John Murray, […], published 1835, →OCLC, page 19:
quote.text: The truth depends on, and is only arrived at, by a legitimate deduction from all the facts which are truly material.

quote.citation: 2014 June 21, “Magician’s brain”, in The Economist‎[1], volume 411, number 8892, archived from the original on 4 November 2018:
quote.text: The truth is that [Isaac] Newton was very much a product of his time. The colossus of science was not the first king of reason, Keynes wrote after reading Newton’s unpublished manuscripts. Instead “he was the last of the magicians”.

definitions.definition: Conformity to fact or reality; correctness, accuracy.

quote.citation: 2012 January, Robert M. Pringle, “How to Be Manipulative”, in American Scientist, volume 100, number 1, page 31:
quote.text: As in much of biology, the most satisfying truths in ecology derive from manipulative experimentation. Tinker with nature and quantify how it responds.

definitions.definition: The state or quality of being true to someone or something.

quote.citation: 1800, S[amuel] T[aylor] Coleridge, “Christabel. Part II.”, in Christabel: Kubla Khan, a Vision: The Pains of Sleep, London:  […]  John Murray, […], by William Bulmer and Co. […], published 1816, →OCLC, page 32:
quote.text: Alas! they had been friends in youth; / But whispering tongues can poison truth;  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A pledge of loyalty or faith.
Conformity to rule; exactness; close correspondence with an example, mood, model, etc.

quote.citation: 1707, J[ohn] Mortimer, The Whole Art of Husbandry; or, The Way of Managing and Improving of Land. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] H[umphreys] for H[enry] Mortlock […], and J[onathan] Robinson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Ploughs,  […]  to make them go true,  […]  depends much upon the truth of the ironwork.

quote.citation: 1840, Joseph Whitworth, A Paper on Plane Metallic Surfaces or True Planes:
quote.text: The process of grinding is, in fact, regarded as indispensable wherever truth is required, yet that of scraping is calculated to produce a higher degree of truth than has ever been attained by grinding.

definitions.definition: That which is real, in a deeper sense; spiritual or ‘genuine’ reality.

quote.citation: 1819 May, John Keats, “Ode on a Grecian Urn”, in Lamia, Isabella, the Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, London:  […]  [Thomas Davison] for Taylor and Hessey, […], published 1820, →OCLC, stanza 5, page 116:
quote.text: "Beauty is truth, truth beauty,"—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.

definitions.definition: (countable) Something acknowledged to be true; a true statement or axiom.

quote.citation: 1813 January 27, [Jane Austen], Pride and Prejudice: […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

definitions.definition: (physics, dated) Topness; the property of a truth quark.
(games) In the game truth or dare, the choice to truthfully answer a question put forth.
(obsolete, transitive) To assert as true; to declare; to speak truthfully.

quote.citation: c. 1636 John Ford, The Fancies Chaste and Noble
quote.text: Had they [the ancients] dreamt this, they would have truthed it heaven.

definitions.definition: To make exact; to correct for inaccuracy.

quote.citation: 1974, Proceedings of the International Symposium on Remote Sensing of Environment, page 226:
quote.text: A concentrated region of the agricultural test area was intensively ground truthed, not only to identify the crop types, but equally important, also to begin to determine the parameters controlling the radar energy reflected from a crop type at a particular stage of growth.

quote.citation: 1990, Advanced Infrared Technology - Part 2, page cxxvi:
quote.text: As is shown in this table, APG images in the validation subset were only truthed with box models, and the 29P images in this subset were never truthed at all.

quote.citation: 2003, Advances in Pattern Recognition ICAPR2003, →ISBN, page 67:
quote.text: This database, which consisists of nearly 180,000 characters, was manually truthed.

quote.citation: 1966, Nancy Sinatra, These Boots Are Made for Walkin':
quote.text: You keep lying, when you oughta be truthin'
